claims.text: Adults need seven or more hours of sleep per night.
claims.explanation: Source 1, Source 2 and Source 3 give the same range of seven or more hours for adults. Source 4 agrees. Source 5 does not address the number.

sources.title: How much sleep do I need?
sources.evidence: Adults aged 18 to 60 should sleep at least 7 hours per night.

sources.title: Sleep deprivation and deficiency
sources.evidence: Most adults need 7 to 9 hours of sleep a day.

sources.title: Healthy sleep
sources.evidence: Experts recommend seven to nine hours for most adults.

sources.title: Sleep
sources.evidence: Recommended sleep for adults is seven to nine hours.

sources.title: Best mattress firmness for side sleepers
sources.evidence: The article covers mattress firmness and does not mention nightly hours.

claims.text: You can fully catch up on lost sleep over the weekend.
claims.explanation: Source 1 reports partial recovery after two nights of extra sleep. Source 2, Source 3 and Source 4 say the effects on metabolism and focus did not fully reverse. Source 5 sides with the claim. The two sides are close, so this is disputed.

sources.title: Recovery sleep after short sleep
sources.evidence: Two nights of extended sleep reversed some measured effects of short sleep.

sources.title: Weekend recovery and metabolism
sources.evidence: Metabolic markers did not fully recover after a weekend of extra sleep.

sources.title: Can you catch up on sleep?
sources.evidence: Catch-up sleep does not erase the effects of a week of short nights.

sources.title: Sleep debt explained
sources.evidence: Recovery sleep improves mood but not long-term health markers.

sources.title: Is weekend sleep worth it?
sources.evidence: Extra weekend sleep can offset some of the fatigue.

claims.text: Eight glasses of water a day is a medical requirement.
claims.explanation: Source 1 finds no evidence for a fixed eight-glass rule. Source 2 and Source 3 say needs vary with body size, diet and climate. Source 4 agrees. Source 5 is about water filters and does not address the claim.

sources.title: Water and healthier drinks
sources.evidence: No study supports a single fixed number of glasses for everyone.

sources.title: Is eight glasses a day a myth?
sources.evidence: Fluid needs vary with body size, diet and climate.

sources.title: Drinking water
sources.evidence: The eight-glass guideline has no clear scientific origin.

sources.title: Do you really need 8 glasses?
sources.evidence: Most people get enough fluid from food and normal thirst.

sources.title: Best water filters this year
sources.evidence: The page compares filters and does not discuss daily intake.

claims.text: Consumer sleep trackers are 95 percent accurate.
claims.explanation: Source 1 says accuracy varies by device and by what is measured. Source 2 and Source 3 give no overall figure, so the 95 percent number cannot be checked.

sources.title: Consumer sleep technology
sources.evidence: Accuracy varies by device and measure, with no overall percentage given.

sources.title: Sleep tracker
sources.evidence: Describes how trackers work but gives no accuracy figure.
